allocation mechanisms

who gets the scarce thing?
Scarce means: not everyone who wants it can have it. So someone or something decides who gets it. That rule is an allocation mechanism.
the rules
price · a test or contest · a government rule · the seller picks · voting
next
four cases: for each, what is the rule?
Your structure (07.10): each case asks 'what is the rule?' with the same five options. Links to scarcity (L01).

what is the rule?

case 1 · ChatGPT Plus

the good
the best model, more messages, faster answers
who gets it
everyone who pays €20 a month
what is the allocation mechanism?
show answer
price
Whoever is willing and able to pay gets it.
It goes to those who value it most in money, and the price tells the seller how much people want it.
Your structure (07.10): each case asks 'what is the rule?' with the same five options.

what is the rule?

case 2 · good grades

supply
teachers give out the good grades
demand
every student wants them
who gets them
those who do best in the exam
what is the allocation mechanism?
show answer
a test or contest (the exam)
Good grades are scarce on purpose: they only mean something if not everyone gets them.
Imagine grades were sold for money: what would a grade then tell an employer?
Your structure (07.10): each case asks 'what is the rule?' with the same five options. Your 'grade market' idea. Discussion question: what goes wrong if grades are allocated by price? (they stop carrying information about ability: signalling).

the job
an internship at a tech firm in Vienna
applicants

who gets it

what is the allocation mechanism?
show answer
the seller picks
The employer chooses among the applicants (CV, interview, tests).
The wage is a price too, but who gets the job is the employer's choice.

a government rule
The city decides how many plates exist; within that limit, a price decides who holds one.
Two mechanisms at once: a rule for the quantity, a market for the plates. More on this in a few slides.

markets

a market is an allocation mechanism too
the rule
sellers offer at a price; buyers decide whether to buy at that price
where
a farmers' market, an app store, a crypto exchange, online worldwide
this course
mostly markets: most economic activity runs through them, and they mostly work well; later: what happens when they fail
Moritz's 'Markets as allocation mechanisms', in our words. To know the allocation in a market you need the price and the quantities: that is what demand and supply give us later today.

perfect competition

the benchmark market
A market is perfectly competitive when all five conditions hold.
1
many small buyers and sellers
2
price takers: no one can move the price
3
identical products: buyers don't care whom they buy from
4
perfect information: everyone knows prices and quality
5
free entry: anyone can start selling
personalise
Personalize this concept using what you know about me.
Based on everything you know about me from our past conversations, give me a 1–2 sentence example of perfect competition from my own life, using the basic concept of perfect competition from an introductory microeconomics class. Choose an example that is genuinely specific to my life rather than a generic example. Make clear a market I buy in and which of the five conditions hold or fail there. Do not explain the concept abstractly—make it concrete and personal to me.

(Your chatbot can draw? Add: "Then draw a simple picture of it.")
Price taker holds for buyers too, and for firms buying their inputs (PS2 Q3).

what is bitcoin mining?

computers compete to write the next page of bitcoin's public notebook, and get paid for it
the notebook
every bitcoin payment is written into one public list; a new page (a block) is added about every 10 minutes
the race
special machines guess numbers billions of times a second; the first correct guess writes the page
the pay
the winner gets 3.125 new bitcoin + the fees that senders attached to their payments
One simple slide (your G3 comment), so students can follow the mining examples. Costs (machines, electricity) come on the barriers slide; the fees come back on L02-12b (who gets into the next block?). Facts: 00_admin/crypto-facts_W02.md.

the guessing race

try it on your phone

the page
the payments + the previous page's fingerprint + one number you choose
scramble it
a fixed formula (SHA-256) turns the page into a code, the hash
the rule
the page only counts if the hash starts with many zeros
the catch
no shortcut: change the number, scramble, check, again and again
Students press [try the next number] a few times (hopeless by hand), then [let my computer guess]: a phone finds 4 zeros in a few seconds (~65,000 tries on average). First to find it raises a hand. Real bitcoin needs ~19 zeros in this notation; all miners together make roughly 10^21 guesses per second. Point: winning = making more guesses = more machines + more electricity. The previous page's fingerprint is inside every page, so changing an old page would mean redoing all the work after it (that's the 'chain'). Correction to a common picture: miners don't make the text 'fit' the next block; they search for the number that makes the hash small.

what is the rule?

case 5 · new bitcoin

the good
3.125 new bitcoin, every ~10 minutes
who gets it
the first miner whose guess makes the hash start with enough zeros
what is the allocation mechanism?
show answer
a contest: proof of work is the rule
Whoever first solves the guessing race gets the new coins.
Your chance of winning = your share of all guesses being made, so more machines (and more electricity) buy more chances.
Your structure (07.10): each case asks 'what is the rule?' with the same five options. Comes right after the mining slides (L02-10, L02-10b). If asked: yes, it works like a lottery where every ticket is a guess and guesses cost electricity.

bitcoin mining

you now know the market: check it against the five conditions

many miners
thousands, but most join one of a few pools
price · product
one world price · a valid page is a valid page
information
prices, difficulty and rewards are public
starting
anyone can plug in a machine, if they have cheap power and €1,000s for machines
which conditions fail? (tap all that apply, then submit)
show answer
two weak spots: many small sellers and free entry
Many small sellers: 3 pools together control more than half (next slides).
Free entry: anyone may start, but cheap electricity and expensive machines are not available to everyone.
Price takers, identical product, information: all fine.

perfect competition

is bitcoin mining a perfect market?

conditiona perfect market would need …bitcoin mining has …
many small sellersthousands of tiny miners, none big enough to matter~ thousands of miners, but 3 pools together control more than half
price takersnobody can move the price✓ one world price for bitcoin; no miner can move it
identical productevery unit the same✓ a valid page is a valid page; one bitcoin = any other
perfect informationeveryone knows prices and rules✓ price, difficulty and rewards are public, live
free entryanyone can start, at the same cost~ anyone can plug in a machine, but cheap electricity and machines (€1,000–4,000 each) are not equally available
verdictclose to perfect, with two weak spots: few big pools, unequal entry
Built row by row: say what the ideal needs, then what mining has. The two weak spots lead to the next slides: barriers to entry (cheap power, capital) and decentralisation (pools).

barriers to entry

what keeps new sellers out
A barrier to entry is anything that makes it hard for a new seller to enter a market.
cheap electricity
miners pay ~€0.05 per kWh in Texas or Paraguay; you pay ~€0.25–0.30 in Vienna
capital
a professional farm runs thousands of machines at ~€1,000–4,000 each
know-how and scale
cooling, buildings, contracts with power plants
better machines
every new generation makes older machines unprofitable
In Frank's terms (Okan): cheap power earns a rent for its owner; the marginal miner earns zero profit. Sources and dates: 00_admin/crypto-facts_W02.md.

monero: the laptop coin

free entry: anyone can mine
monero
a cryptocurrency designed so that normal computer chips (CPUs) can mine it
your laptop
a few thousand guesses per second → roughly 10 cents of monero a day
your electricity
a laptop running all day ≈ 1 kWh ≈ €0.25–0.30 in Vienna
would mining monero on your laptop make you money?
show answer
no
The coins are worth less than the electricity (and the laptop gets hot).
Entry is free, but only miners with cheap power make money: in the long run, entry competes profit away.
Rough numbers; re-check the monero price and pool data on the morning of the lecture. Monero machines (ASICs) now exist too, so even here the CPU advantage is eroding.

how many sellers really decide?

count the players who control more than half
The Nakamoto coefficient: the smallest number of players who together control more than half of all mining. Perfect competition needs this number to be large.
why pools
a single miner wins a page very rarely, so miners team up in pools and share the prizes
bitcoin pools
Foundry 24% · AntPool 21% · F2Pool 16% · many smaller ones
how many bitcoin pools together control more than half?
show answer
3
Add the biggest until you pass 50%: 24 + 21 = 45% is not yet half; + 16 = 61%.
So 'many small sellers' is the weak spot: thousands of miners, but 3 pools decide which payments go into the pages.
Monero, the coin anyone can mine on a laptop: one pool alone had 36–53% in early 2026 → its number is 1–2. Free entry alone does not give you many small sellers.
Foundry 24
+ AntPool 21  = 45  (< 50)
+ F2Pool 16   = 61  (> 50)  → 3 pools
Srinivasan & Lee (2017) defined the coefficient. Pool shares change daily: re-check on the day (hashrateindex, miningpoolstats). Caveat if asked: a pool is not one owner; miners can switch pools within minutes, which limits what a pool can do.

many sellers, but not super many: 3 countries mine two thirds
why there
electricity is the biggest cost: cheap gas, hydro, cold climates
energy
~140–175 TWh a year ≈ 0.5% of the world's electricity (≈ 2× Austria)
for perfect competition
thousands of miners, but packed into a few countries: one government's rules can move a big part of the market (China's 2021 ban moved half the miners abroad)
USA36.7%
Russia17.2%
China12.2%
Paraguay4.7%
UAE3%
Oman2.8%
Canada2.6%
Ethiopia2.4%
Indonesia1.8%
Norway1.7%
all others14.9%
share of all bitcoin mining, Q3 2026 (Hashrate Index; estimates)
Your framing (07.10): many sellers, but not super many. Bars = share of all mining, not scaled to the largest. Country figures are estimates (pool IP addresses are not where machines stand; hidden mining in ban countries). Kazakhstan (~18% in 2021) is no longer in the top 10. Austria uses roughly 70 TWh a year: check before class. Source: 00_admin/crypto-facts_W02.md.

taxi licences

many sellers behind a fence
istanbul
about 17,400 taxi plates: the same number from 1990 for about 30 years
a plate
trades for about €200,000 (₺11.25 million, October 2026)
for scale
minimum wage ≈ €510 a month · average rent ≈ €820 · a latte ≈ €2.90 → a plate ≈ 33 years of minimum wage
the fare
set by the city, not by the market: €1.30 to start + €0.87 per km
newcomers
the city asked for 5,000 new taxis; rejected 11 times · Uber may only work with licensed taxis
Not a monopoly: thousands of owners and drivers. But nobody new may enter, and the price is fixed. Introduce slowly, then check the five conditions. Facts with sources: 00_admin/market-examples-facts_W02.md.

the fare

costs about €200,000 (≈ 33 years of Turkish minimum wage), far more than the car
2024
the city announced 2,500 extra plates · within days plate prices fell about 6%
new york
a taxi licence: $200,000 (2002) → $1.3 million (2014) → down about 90% when ride apps came

what would make it a perfect market?
free entry
anyone with a safe car and a clean record can drive: the licence checks quality but does not cap the number

fares set by supply and demand; apps show the price before the ride (information)

Normative side (L01: positive vs normative): drivers who borrowed to buy plates lose; safety and income are real concerns. The economics is positive: what happens to prices and quantities.

selling answers

the other AI market: inference as a service

inference
using a trained model: every time you send a prompt, a server computes the answer
open models
some top models can be downloaded by anyone (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi)
the sellers
about 10 firms run the SAME model and sell answers per million tokens (word pieces), plus the lab's own service
you buy
from whoever is cheapest or fastest; comparison sites list them side by side
Contrast with building the model (L02-19a/b): building = a few labs; selling answers from an open model = many sellers. Source: bycloud, 'The Strange Economics of LLM Inference-as-a-Service' (YouTube, 29.09.2026); numbers are the video's, say 'according to one analysis'. Facts: 00_admin/market-examples-facts_W02.md.

selling answers

one server, one hour

cost
rent 8 top GPUs: about $6 each → $48 an hour
price
the market price for this model ≈ $7 per million answer tokens
speed
a simple setup makes about 3.2 million tokens an hour
revenue
3.2 × $7 ≈ $22 an hour
a host loses about $25 an hour. what can it do?
show answer
serve faster on the same GPUs
It can't raise the price: ten others sell the same model. Customers would leave.
Renting more GPUs only multiplies the loss.
Only lower cost per token helps: it needs about 2,000 tokens a second (6.9 million an hour) to break even. That is competition: the price is pushed down to the cost of the best sellers.
revenue  3.24 m tokens × $6.96 ≈ $22.55 an hour
cost     8 GPUs × $6      = $48 an hour
break-even: 48 / 6.96 ≈ 6.9 m tokens an hour ≈ 1,900 a second
Source: bycloud, 'The Strange Economics of LLM Inference-as-a-Service' (YouTube, 29.09.2026); numbers are the video's, say 'according to one analysis'. Facts: 00_admin/market-examples-facts_W02.md.

inference as a service: which conditions fail?

sellers
about 10 hosts per open model, plus the lab itself
the product
the same model, but some hosts are faster or more reliable
prices
listed side by side
starting

which conditions fail? (tap all that apply, then submit)
show answer

Many sellers, price takers, information: fine.

selling answers

is inference as a service a perfect market?

conditiona perfect market would need …selling answers has …
many small sellersmany sellers✓ about 10 hosts per open model, plus the lab itself
price takersnobody can move the price✓ charge more than the others and customers leave
identical productevery unit the same~ the same model, but speed and reliability differ; special chips (Groq, Cerebras) are 3× faster
perfect informationeveryone knows the prices✓ prices listed side by side
free entryanyone can start, at the same cost~ anyone can rent GPUs, but the lab that built the model is cheaper: it knows its model and gets it first; bigger hosts are cheaper per token
verdictclose to perfect: thin margins, prices near cost; the weak spot is unequal costs
Built row by row. Lesson for Thursday: when many sell the same thing, the price is pushed to the cost of the cheapest sellers; those with a cost edge (the lab, the big hosts) earn the profit. Source: bycloud, 'The Strange Economics of LLM Inference-as-a-Service' (YouTube, 29.09.2026); numbers are the video's, say 'according to one analysis'. Facts: 00_admin/market-examples-facts_W02.md.

demand

price ↓ → more buyers
Demand: how much buyers want to buy at each price.
as a function
QD = f(P): pick a price, get the quantity demanded
read across →
at €20, 20 of you buy

The demand curve = everyone's reservation prices sorted from highest to lowest. Read up = the willingness to pay of the marginal (last) buyer. Can's bedtime PDF from Raif explains this view in detail.

law of demand

price ↑ → quantity ↓
When a good's price rises, people buy less of it, all else equal.
demand form
price ↑ → quantity demanded ↓ (all else equal)
inverse form
the marginal willingness to pay falls as more is sold · your class: the 1st buyer would pay €100, the 20th €20, the 38th €5
why
each extra unit is worth less to a buyer; at a higher price more reservation prices fall below it
the picture
a downward-sloping (inverse) demand curve
'All else equal' prepares Thursday: when something else changes, the whole curve moves.

shift or movement?

news
a cloud-storage plan changes its price from €10 to €3 a month
you
you upload all your photos
in the market for this plan, this is …
show answer
a movement along the demand curve: the quantity demanded rises
The good's OWN price changed, so you move along the demand curve.
'Demand' (the whole curve) only shifts when something other than the own price changes.
Written by Alper, checked by Sinan against every graded item (PASS, 06.10). This previews Thursday's shift vs movement; the exams test exactly this wording (midterm). If you'd rather keep all of 'shift vs movement' for Thursday, drop this slide.

supply

price ↑ → more is offered
Supply: how much sellers want to sell at each price. It slopes up because the next unit costs more to provide.
any firm
producing more needs overtime, extra staff, new machines: each extra unit costs more (rising marginal cost)
bitcoin miners
when bitcoin is cheap, only the newest, most efficient machines are worth running; when it's expensive, even old machines are switched back on
used machines
the higher the resale price, the more miners sell their old machine instead of running it
personalise

Do not explain the concept abstractly—make it concrete and personal to me.

Rising marginal cost: each extra unit comes from a less efficient machine / an owner who values the machine more. Mirror of the demand slide.

Your sequence (07.10), after Raif's HowMarketsFindEquilibrium.pdf, scaled to values 10–100. Buyers' values = their reservation prices (demand); sellers' costs = the lowest price they accept (supply). Two rows, revealed one by one.

Each buyer pays exactly what the good is worth to them; each seller gets exactly their cost.
Ten trades, and nobody is better off: more trades is not the same as more value.
Your sequence (07.10), after Raif's HowMarketsFindEquilibrium.pdf, scaled to values 10–100. Gain of a trade = buyer's value − seller's cost.

gain9070503010−10 ✗
how many of these pairs should trade?
show answer
5 pairs · total gain €250
The 6th pair (buyer €50, seller €60) would lose €10: stop before it.
This is the most value any matching can create.
90 + 70 + 50 + 30 + 10 = €250
(= the 5 highest values 400 − the 5 lowest costs 150)
Your sequence (07.10), after Raif's HowMarketsFindEquilibrium.pdf, scaled to values 10–100.

who gets the €250? (1)

pair100–1090–2080–3070–4060–50

who gets the €250? (3)

the pair
buyer €100 and seller €10
they agree on
€40
how much value does this trade create?
show answer
€90 (same as at €100 or at €10)
Buyer gains 100 − 40 = 60, seller gains 40 − 10 = 30: together 90.
The price only splits the gain between the two; the total does not depend on it.
buyer 100 − 40 = 60
seller 40 − 10 = 30
total 60 + 30 = 90 = 100 − 10
Any price between a pair's cost and value creates the same total; only the split changes. So all five pairs together still create €250, whatever the prices.

who stays out

not trading can be the right answer
buyers who stay out
€50, €40, €30, €20, €10: they don't value it enough
sellers who stay out
€60, €70, €80, €90, €100: they are too expensive
if they traded anyway
buyer €50 with seller €60 would destroy €10
Value is created by the right people trading, not by everyone trading.

one price for everyone

in a market, everyone pays the same price

price€30€50€55€60€80
buyers who want to buy (value ≥ price)86553
sellers who want to sell (cost ≤ price)35568
which single price makes buyers = sellers?
show answer
€55 (any price from €50 to €60 works; €55 is the middle)
At €55: 5 buyers (values 100 … 60) and 5 sellers (costs 10 … 50): exactly the 5 best pairs trade, €250 is created.
Below €50 too many buyers, too few sellers; above €60 the opposite.
This previews Thursday's equilibrium. At exactly €50 the €50-buyer is indifferent; at exactly €60 the €60-seller is.

Clearly an invented illustration. Early prices scatter, later ones bunch near 55, because traders who paid or got a 'bad' price look elsewhere. Bora (LLM trading floor) builds a real replay with AI traders for a later class.

marginal buyer · marginal seller

two people pin down the price
marginal buyer
the last buyer who still buys: value €60 → the price can't go above €60
marginal seller
the last seller who still sells: cost €50 → the price can't go below €50
everyone else
buyer €100's value doesn't push the price up: it only decides that she buys
who decides where the price lands?
show answer
the marginal buyer (€60) and the marginal seller (€50)
The price lies between them: €50–€60.
The first buyer and seller who stay out (€50 and €60) hold it there from the other side.
Raif's PDF: Böhm-Bawerk's 'marginal pairs' (1889). Value of the last unit bought and cost of the last unit sold.

summary

allocation mechanisms
the rule for who gets scarce things: price, a test, a government rule, the seller picks · markets use prices
perfect competition
many small sellers · price takers · identical · informed · free entry
barriers to entry
what keeps new sellers out (cheap power, capital)
decentralisation
how many players control more than half
demand
how much buyers want at each price; slopes down
inverse demand
what the buyer of the Q-th unit would pay at most
supply / inverse supply
how much is offered at each price · the lowest price for the Q-th unit
